explanation_text: On a cuckoo clock face, the same digit means different things depending on where it sits — the 1 near the top marks a different hour than a 1 lower down, just as a digit's place gives it its value.

explanation_text: When more pretzels are added to a stand's basket, the total grows; when a customer buys some and they are lifted out, the total shrinks — that is addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a wooden pretzel basket at an Oktoberfest stand being filled (count rising) and emptied (count falling), with the totals shown above.

explanation_text: Lining bratwurst up in equal rows on a grill shows multiplication — 3 rows of 4 sausages is 12. Sharing them out evenly onto plates shows division.
image_prompt: Show bratwurst arranged in equal rows on a grill (multiplication), then divided evenly onto plates (division).

explanation_text: When decorated Easter eggs are placed in pairs, every egg has a partner and the count is even. If one egg is left single, the count is odd.
image_prompt: Show painted Easter eggs arranged in pairs, with one single egg left over to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: The white and blue diamonds of the Bavarian flag repeat in a steady rhythm — counting every third diamond mirrors counting by 3s, just like skip counting.
image_prompt: Show the repeating white-and-blue diamond pattern of the Bavarian flag, highlighting every third diamond to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: Comparing two stacks of pretzels at a market stall shows which has more and which has fewer — the same idea as greater than and less than for numbers.
image_prompt: Show two stacks of pretzels of different heights at a German market stall with > and < symbols between them.

german_culture: Estimating guests in a festival tent
explanation_text: When planning a festival tent, hosts estimate the number of guests to the nearest ten — that is rounding, making a messy number easier to work with.
image_prompt: Show an Oktoberfest tent host estimating guest numbers, with approximate counts rounded to the nearest ten.

explanation_text: When one big pretzel is broken into four equal pieces and shared, each friend receives one part of the whole — a fraction of the pretzel.
image_prompt: Show a large pretzel divided into four equal pieces, each labeled as a fraction of the whole pretzel.

explanation_text: A Black Forest cake cut into 2 big slices or 4 smaller slices still gives the same total cake — the fractions 1/2 and 2/4 describe the same amount.
image_prompt: Show a round Black Forest cake divided first into halves, then into quarters, demonstrating that equal amounts are equivalent fractions.

explanation_text: Two quarters of a pretzel can be pushed together to make one half — writing 2/4 as 1/2 is simplifying the fraction to its lowest terms.
image_prompt: Show two pretzel quarters joining to form half a pretzel, labeled 2/4 becoming 1/2.

explanation_text: If a baker has 3 full loaves of bread and half a loaf more, the amount is 3½ — a whole number joined with a fraction, called a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three whole bread loaves and one half-loaf, labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When rolls fill more than one full tray, the amount can be written as parts of a single tray size — a fraction with a numerator larger than its denominator, an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show bread rolls spilling past a full tray, symbolizing fractions with a value greater than 1.

german_culture: Stacking cake slices on one plate
explanation_text: Placing slices of Black Forest cake from different plates onto one plate shows how fractional parts add together into a larger portion.
image_prompt: Show separate cake slices being moved onto one plate, illustrating how fractions combine through addition.

german_culture: Slicing a piece of the cake away
explanation_text: Cutting and removing a slice from a Black Forest cake leaves a smaller portion — the cake left over is what remains after subtracting a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a Black Forest cake with one slice removed, the remaining portion labeled as the fraction left.

german_culture: Half of half a cake slice
explanation_text: If a cake slice is halved and one of those halves is halved again, you get a quarter of the original — finding a fraction of a fraction is multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a cake slice divided in half, and one half divided again to reveal a quarter, labeled with fractions.

explanation_text: If one bratwurst is cut into thirds, the question of how many thirds fit into one sausage shows division of a whole by a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a bratwurst being cut into three equal parts to illustrate dividing by a fraction.

explanation_text: A German bakery scale records 1.5 kilograms of flour — the decimal point splits whole kilograms from tenths, just as digits after the point show tenths and hundredths.
image_prompt: Show a bakery scale marked 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 kilograms of flour.

german_culture: Measuring jugs for milk and dough
explanation_text: Half a liter poured from a German measuring jug and 0.5 liters are the same amount — converting between fractions and decimals changes only how it is written.
image_prompt: Show two measuring jugs, one labeled ½ and the other 0.5, filled with the same amount.

explanation_text: If a student answers 92 of 100 questions correctly on a German school test, the score is 92% — a percent expresses a part out of one hundred.
image_prompt: Show a graded German school test with 92/100 written and a 92% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A sign reading '30% off' on a wooden ornament at a Christmas market shows how a percent finds a part of a price.
image_prompt: Show a Christmas market stall sign with a wooden ornament marked 30% off and a reduced price tag.

explanation_text: If the pine-cone weight of a cuckoo clock is unlabeled, its value is unknown until measured — an unknown quantity is a variable.
image_prompt: Show cuckoo clock weights, some labeled with numbers and one unlabeled marked with the letter x.

explanation_text: Two labeled weights hanging beside one unlabeled weight give 2 + x — an expression combining known numbers and a variable.
image_prompt: Show two labeled cuckoo clock weights plus one unlabeled weight, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: A cuckoo clock runs evenly when its two hanging weights are equal, just as an equation holds true when both sides are balanced.
image_prompt: Show a cuckoo clock with two hanging weights of equal size, labeled as two sides of an equation.

explanation_text: To make the clock run correctly you change just one weight — adding or removing it to reach balance is solving a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a hand adjusting a single cuckoo clock weight to restore balance, representing a one-step equation.

explanation_text: Kneading the dough and then shaping the pretzel must happen in two clear steps, just like solving an equation that needs two operations.
image_prompt: Show the two-step sequence of kneading dough and then shaping a pretzel, symbolizing two-step equation solving.

explanation_text: When one bratwurst stand sells more sausages than another, the comparison is unequal — exactly the idea behind greater than and less than.
image_prompt: Show two bratwurst stands with different numbers of sausages and > or < symbols between them.

explanation_text: A Black Forest cake is layered in a strict order — sponge, cream, cherries — and the order matters, just as the order of operations decides which math step comes first.
image_prompt: Show the strict layering sequence of a Black Forest cake, with each step labeled like operations in PEMDAS.

explanation_text: If a cuckoo clock weight is lost, an identical replacement keeps the clock running — replacing one known value with another is substitution.
image_prompt: Show a missing cuckoo clock weight being replaced with an identical one, representing substitution.

german_culture: Pins on a German railway map
explanation_text: Each pin on a railway map marks one station — a single location, just as a point marks one position in geometry.
image_prompt: Show a German railway map with pins at stations, each marked as a point.

explanation_text: A straight stretch of Autobahn appears to continue in both directions without end — the same idea as a geometric line.
image_prompt: Show a straight Autobahn section stretching to the horizon, represented as a geometric line.

explanation_text: The pendulum of a cuckoo clock swings from side to side, and the gap between its resting position and a swing is an angle.
image_prompt: Show a cuckoo clock pendulum swung to one side with the angle from the vertical clearly marked.

explanation_text: In a half-timbered house, upright and cross beams meet at right angles — lines that cross at 90° are perpendicular.
image_prompt: Show the timber frame of a half-timbered (Fachwerk) house with beams meeting at right angles.

german_culture: Railway tracks running side by side
explanation_text: The two rails of a German railway line run side by side and never meet — they stay the same distance apart, like parallel lines.
image_prompt: Show two railway tracks running parallel into the distance, always the same distance apart.

explanation_text: The timber and plaster panels on a half-timbered house form closed shapes with straight sides — closed many-sided figures are polygons.
image_prompt: Show the geometric panels of a half-timbered facade, each shape outlined as a polygon.

explanation_text: The gable (roof triangle) of a Bavarian alpine house is a closed shape with three sides — a triangle.
image_prompt: Show the triangular gable ends of Bavarian alpine houses, each outlined as a triangle.

explanation_text: The timber frame of a half-timbered wall creates squares and rectangles — four-sided closed shapes, or quadrilaterals.

german_culture: Walking the boundary of a market square
explanation_text: Strolling around the edge of a medieval market square measures the distance around it — the perimeter of the shape.

german_culture: Picnic blanket in a beer garden
explanation_text: The amount of grass a blanket covers inside a beer garden is the blanket's area.

german_culture: Water barrels in a Bavarian courtyard
explanation_text: The amount of water a wooden barrel can hold is its volume, measured in liters.

german_culture: Front view of a cuckoo clock
explanation_text: Viewed from the front, a cuckoo clock's face is a circle, so its radius, diameter, and circumference can be measured and labeled.

explanation_text: Dividing the circumference of a round Black Forest cake by its diameter always gives the same ratio — the constant pi (π ≈ 3.14).

explanation_text: A Christmas market laid out in rows and columns is a coordinate grid, and each stall sits at its own intersection — like points on a coordinate plane.

german_culture: Locating stalls on a market map
explanation_text: Marking each stall's position on a market map places it at an exact coordinate — plotting points on a coordinate plane.

explanation_text: The Brandenburg Gate is built so that its left and right halves mirror each other exactly across the center — reflection symmetry.

german_culture: Carousel horses at a German fair
explanation_text: As a fairground carousel turns, the horses rotate and shift position while keeping their shape — geometric transformations.

explanation_text: Pretzel dough keeps a fixed balance of flour to water — a ratio such as 3 parts flour to 1 part water, written 3:1.

explanation_text: A souvenir model of Neuschwanstein Castle is a smaller copy with every length reduced by the same factor — keeping the proportions.

german_culture: Autobahn speed in kilometers per hour

german_culture: Middle house price on a German street
explanation_text: When the house prices on a street are lined up from lowest to highest, the price in the exact middle is the median.

explanation_text: If more customers buy sourdough than any other bread in the bakery, sourdough is the most frequent value — the mode.

explanation_text: The gap between the day with the most visitors and the day with the fewest shows the range of the data.

german_culture: Tracking café sales over the months
